title: Prenatal vitamins
usage: Use as after-visit instructions about prenatal vitamins and folic acid.
cerner_text:
Prenatal vitamins

Folic acid is the most important part. Take 400 to 800 mcg every day. It helps prevent birth defects of the brain and spine. Your dose: _

Iron helps your blood. Iodine, vitamin D, calcium, and DHA are also helpful.

If your vitamin makes you sick:

- Take it at night, or with food.
- Ask us about a vitamin with less iron.
- Gummy vitamins are easier to take, but most have no iron. You may need iron separately.
- A vitamin you can keep down is better than one you cannot.

Store-brand vitamins work as well as expensive ones.

Do not take extra vitamin A. Do not take 2 prenatal vitamins to get more of something.

Bring all your supplements and herbal products to your next visit.

Call the clinic if you cannot keep any vitamin down, or cost is a problem.

title: Food safety in pregnancy
usage: Use as after-visit instructions about food safety and infection prevention.
cerner_text:
Food safety in pregnancy

Some germs in food can harm your baby. Listeria is rare but serious.

Avoid:

- Deli meat and hot dogs unless heated until steaming
- Unpasteurized milk, cheese, and juice
- Raw or undercooked meat, eggs, and seafood
- Refrigerated smoked fish unless cooked in a dish
- Raw sprouts

Safe:

- Pasteurized cheese, like cottage, cream, string, feta, and mozzarella. Queso fresco and similar fresh cheeses are safe only if heated until steaming.
- Meat, eggs, and fish cooked all the way through

Other tips:

- Wash fruits and vegetables well.
- Wash hands and cutting boards after touching raw meat.
- Have someone else change the cat litter. If you must, wear gloves and wash your hands.
- Wear gloves when gardening.

Call the clinic if you have fever, muscle aches, or diarrhea after eating a risky food.

title: Fish in pregnancy
usage: Use as after-visit instructions about fish and mercury.
cerner_text:
Fish in pregnancy

Fish is good for you and your baby's brain and eyes. Eat 2 to 3 servings a week, about 8 to 12 ounces total. Some fish have mercury, which can harm your baby.

Best choices:

- Salmon, sardines, trout, tilapia, cod, catfish, and pollock
- Canned light tuna, shrimp, crab, and scallops

Once a week at most:

- Albacore or white tuna, halibut, grouper, and Chilean sea bass

Do not eat:

- Shark, swordfish, king mackerel, tilefish from the Gulf of Mexico, marlin, orange roughy, and bigeye tuna

Cook fish until it flakes apart. Avoid raw fish, like sushi with raw fish.

If you catch your own fish, check your state advice for those waters.

Call the clinic with questions about a fish not on this list.

title: Is it safe in pregnancy
usage: Use as answers to common "is it safe" questions in pregnancy.
cerner_text:
Is it safe in pregnancy?

Caffeine: yes, less than 200 mg a day. That is about one 12-ounce cup of coffee. Tea, soda, and chocolate count too.

Hair dye: yes. Very little gets through your scalp. If you are worried, wait until after 13 weeks.

Baths: warm baths are fine. Avoid hot tubs and saunas, especially in the first 3 months.

Sex: yes, in a normal pregnancy. It does not cause miscarriage or early labor. We will tell you if you need to avoid it.

Exercise: yes. It does not cause miscarriage. Aim for 150 minutes a week.

Eating for two: no need. You need no extra calories in the first 3 months. Add about 340 calories a day in the middle 3 months. Add about 450 a day in the last 3 months.

Medicines: acetaminophen is the pain medicine of choice. Do not take ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin unless we tell you to. Ask us before taking any new medicine or herbal product.

Call the clinic with any other questions.

Vaccines in pregnancy protect you, and they pass protection to your baby.

Recommended:

- Tdap, for whooping cough, at 27 to 36 weeks in every pregnancy. Your baby is born with protection.
- Flu shot, in any trimester during flu season. Use the shot, not the nose spray.
- RSV vaccine at 32 to 36 weeks during RSV season, or an RSV shot for your baby after birth. Your baby needs one or the other, not both. Your plan: _
- COVID-19 vaccine: _

Wait until after birth:

- MMR and chickenpox vaccines are not given in pregnancy. If you are not immune, you can get them before you leave the hospital. They are safe while breastfeeding.

title: Alcohol in pregnancy
usage: Use as after-visit instructions about alcohol in pregnancy.
cerner_text:
Alcohol in pregnancy

No amount of alcohol is known to be safe in pregnancy. The safest choice is not to drink.

Heavy drinking and binge drinking can cause lifelong problems for your baby. These problems can be prevented.

If you drank before you knew you were pregnant, this is very common. Tell us how much so we know what to watch for.

If you drink every day, do not stop suddenly on your own. Stopping suddenly can be dangerous. We can help you stop safely.

Call the clinic if you need help cutting back or stopping.

Go to the ER if you have shaking, sweating, seeing things, or a seizure after stopping.

title: Smoking, vaping, and cannabis in pregnancy
usage: Use as after-visit instructions about tobacco, vaping, and cannabis in pregnancy.
cerner_text:
Smoking, vaping, and cannabis in pregnancy

Quitting helps at any point in pregnancy. The sooner the better.

Smoking and vaping:

- Lower the blood flow to your baby
- Raise the risk of a small baby, early birth, stillbirth, and SIDS
- Vaping is not safe. Nicotine itself is harmful.

Cannabis:

- Crosses to your baby in any form, smoked, vaped, or eaten
- Is linked to small babies and learning problems later
- Is not a safe treatment for nausea. We have better options.

After birth, keep your home and car smoke-free. Smoke on clothes and hair also harms babies.

Help to quit: _. Free help: call 1-800-QUIT-NOW.

Call the clinic if you want help quitting.

title: Exercise in pregnancy
usage: Use as after-visit instructions about exercise in pregnancy.
cerner_text:
Exercise in pregnancy

Exercise is safe and healthy for most pregnancies. Aim for 150 minutes a week, like 30 minutes on 5 days.

Exercise helps:

- Back pain, swelling, and constipation
- Sleep, mood, and energy
- Lower the risk of gestational diabetes and high blood pressure

Good choices:

- Walking
- Swimming and water exercise
- Prenatal yoga
- Stationary bike
- Light weights. Do not hold your breath.
- Kegels, 3 sets of 10 every day

Avoid:

- Lying flat on your back for a long time after 13 weeks
- Contact sports and activities where you could fall
- Scuba diving
- Hot yoga or exercise in high heat

You should be able to talk while you exercise. If you cannot, slow down.

Stop exercising. Call the clinic if you have:

- Bleeding or leaking fluid
- Dizziness or chest pain
- Bad shortness of breath
- Regular contractions
- Less movement from your baby
- Calf pain or swelling

title: Common discomforts of pregnancy
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for heartburn, aches, hemorrhoids, sleep, and swelling in pregnancy.
cerner_text:
Common discomforts of pregnancy

These are common and not dangerous. Here is what helps.

Heartburn:

- Eat small meals. Do not eat 3 hours before lying down.
- Raise the head of your bed.
- Tums are safe. Ask us if you need more.

Sharp pain low on one side:

- This is often stretching of the ligaments that hold the uterus.
- Move slowly when you stand or roll over. Use warmth.

Constipation and hemorrhoids:

- Drink water, eat fiber, and move every day.
- Put your feet on a stool when you sit on the toilet. Do not strain.
- Witch hazel pads and warm sitz baths help.

Back pain:

- Wear flat shoes. Use a pillow between your knees at night.
- A belly support belt helps some people.

Sleep:

- Sleep on either side after 20 weeks. If you wake up on your back, just turn over.
- Stretch your calves for leg cramps.

Swelling in the feet:

- Put your feet up. Wear compression socks.

Call the clinic if you have:

- Sudden swelling of the face or hands
- One calf that is swollen, painful, or warm
- Belly pain that does not go away, or comes with bleeding, fever, or regular tightening
- Burning when you pee

usage: Use as after-visit instructions about depression and anxiety in pregnancy.
cerner_text:
Mood in pregnancy

Depression and anxiety are common in pregnancy. They are not your fault, and they can be treated.

Tell us if you have:

- Low mood most days
- Lost interest in things you enjoy
- Worry that will not stop, or scary thoughts that pop into your head
- Trouble sleeping even when you can
- Any thoughts of hurting yourself

Treatment helps you and your baby. Untreated depression raises the risk of early birth and depression after birth.

What helps:

- Counseling, alone or with medicine
- Several medicines are safe in pregnancy. If you stopped a medicine when you got pregnant, tell us.
- Sleep, sunlight, exercise, and time with people who support you

Your plan: _

Call or text the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline any time: 1-833-TLC-MAMA, which is 1-833-852-6262.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, call or text 988. Call 911 if you are in danger right now.

Preeclampsia is high blood pressure in pregnancy that can affect your organs and your baby. It usually starts after 20 weeks. It can also start in the first weeks after birth. Finding it early helps.

Low-dose aspirin can lower your risk. Your plan: _

Your blood pressure today: _
Next blood pressure check: _

Go to L&D or the ER right away if you have:

- A headache that will not go away with acetaminophen
- Vision changes, like spots or flashing lights
- Pain under your right ribs or high in your belly
- Sudden swelling of your face or hands
- Trouble breathing
- Blood pressure of 160 over 110 or higher

Call the clinic the same day if your blood pressure is 140 over 90 or higher.

After your baby is born, these signs still matter. Do not wait for your postpartum visit.

title: Kick counts
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for fetal movement counting.
cerner_text:
Kick counts

After 28 weeks, count your baby's movements every day. You learn what is normal for your baby.

How to count:

- Pick a time when your baby is usually active, like after a meal.
- Lie on your side or sit with your feet up.
- Count kicks, rolls, and jabs. Hiccups do not count.
- Most babies move 10 times in less than 2 hours, often much faster.

title: Signs of labor
usage: Use as after-visit instructions about when to go to L&D.
cerner_text:
Signs of labor: when to go in

True labor:

- Contractions get longer, stronger, and closer together.
- They do not stop when you rest or change position.
- Pain often starts in the back and moves to the front.

False labor:

- Contractions are uneven and do not get stronger.
- They often stop with rest, water, or a change in position.

When to go to the hospital:

- First baby: contractions 5 minutes apart, lasting 1 minute each, for 1 hour.
- Second or later baby: go sooner, when contractions are 6 to 8 minutes apart.

Go in right away if:

- Your water breaks, as a gush or a steady trickle
- You have bright red bleeding, more than spotting
- Your baby moves less than usual
- You have bad belly pain that does not stop
- You have a bad headache, vision changes, or sudden swelling

Early labor is often more comfortable at home. Try a warm shower, walking, rest, fluids, and a light snack.

Call L&D with questions: _

- Leaking fluid from your vagina
- Bleeding or spotting
- Change in discharge, like watery, mucus, or bloody

title: Bleeding in early pregnancy
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for bleeding or cramping in early pregnancy.
cerner_text:
Bleeding in early pregnancy

Light spotting in early pregnancy is common and often normal. Sometimes it is a sign of miscarriage or a pregnancy outside the uterus, called an ectopic pregnancy.

Your plan:

- Blood test or ultrasound on _
- Use pads, not tampons, so you can see how much you bleed.
- Rest as you feel you need. Activity does not cause miscarriage.

Call the clinic if:

- Bleeding gets heavier or does not stop
- Cramping gets worse
- You pass tissue

Go to the ER right away if you have:

- Bleeding that soaks 2 pads an hour for 2 hours
- Bad pain, especially on one side of your belly
- Pain in your shoulder tip
- Dizziness or fainting
- Fever

If your blood type is Rh negative, you may need a shot. Tell any ER you visit.

title: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy.
cerner_text:
Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

Nausea is very common in early pregnancy. It usually gets better by 14 to 16 weeks.

What helps:

- Eat small snacks every 1 to 2 hours. Do not let your stomach get empty.
- Keep crackers by your bed. Eat a few before you get up.
- Eat foods that sound good, even if they are plain.
- Sip fluids between meals, not with meals.
- Try ginger tea, ginger candy, or ginger capsules.
- Avoid smells that bother you.
- Take your prenatal vitamin at night, or switch to one without iron.

Medicine:

- Vitamin B6, 25 mg by mouth 3 times a day
- You can add doxylamine, 12.5 mg by mouth at bedtime. It can make you sleepy.
- Other medicine: _

Call the clinic if you cannot keep any food down for 1 day, or you are losing weight.

Go to the ER if you:

- Cannot keep fluids down
- Have not peed in 8 hours
- Vomit blood
- Feel faint

title: Gestational diabetes
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for gestational diabetes.
cerner_text:
Gestational diabetes

Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar that starts in pregnancy. With good care, most people have healthy babies.

Check your blood sugar:

- When you wake up, before eating. Goal: below 95.
- 1 hour after each meal. Goal: below 140.
- Or 2 hours after each meal. Goal: below 120.
- Write down every number and bring your log to every visit.

Food:

- Eat 3 small meals and 2 to 3 snacks a day.
- Eat protein with every meal and snack.
- Limit bread, rice, pasta, potatoes, and sweets. Choose whole grains.
- Do not drink juice, soda, or sweet tea.

Walk for 10 to 15 minutes after meals. It lowers your blood sugar.

Medicine: _

You may need extra ultrasounds and baby heart rate checks later in pregnancy.

After birth, you need a sugar test at 4 to 12 weeks. Your risk of type 2 diabetes stays higher for life, so get checked every 1 to 3 years.

Call the clinic if:

- Your numbers are above goal 2 or more times in a week
- Your sugar is below 70

title: Pain relief in labor
usage: Use as after-visit instructions about labor pain relief options.
cerner_text:
Pain relief in labor

There is no right way to manage labor pain. You can change your mind at any time.

Without medicine:

- Warm shower or tub
- Walking, rocking, a birthing ball, or changing positions
- Slow breathing
- Firm pressure on your lower back
- Heat on your back and cool cloths on your face

With medicine:

- Nitrous oxide, or laughing gas. You hold the mask. It takes the edge off and wears off in minutes.
- IV pain medicine. It takes the edge off but can make you and your baby sleepy.
- Epidural. This is the strongest pain relief. A thin tube in your lower back numbs the pain. You stay awake.

Epidural facts:

- It does not raise your chance of a C-section.
- Pushing may take longer.
- You will have an IV and a monitor on your belly.

Your preferences: _

title: Birth after a C-section
usage: Use as after-visit instructions about VBAC and repeat cesarean.
cerner_text:
Birth after a C-section

Many people who had 1 C-section can safely try a vaginal birth. This is called VBAC.

About 60 to 80 out of 100 people who try VBAC succeed.

Things that affect your chances:

- The reason for your last C-section
- The type of cut on your uterus
- Whether you have had a vaginal birth before
- Your health in this pregnancy
- Whether the hospital can do an emergency C-section any time

Risks of VBAC: a small chance that the scar on your uterus opens in labor, less than 1 in 100. This can be serious, which is why labor is watched closely.

Risks of repeat C-section: surgery risks, a longer recovery, and more risk with each future pregnancy.

Your plan: _

Call the clinic if you want to talk more about your options.

title: Constipation in pregnancy
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for constipation in pregnancy.
cerner_text:
Constipation in pregnancy

Constipation is common in pregnancy. Hormones slow your bowels, and iron pills can make it worse.

What helps:

- Drink 8 to 10 cups of water a day.
- Eat fruits, vegetables, beans, prunes, and whole grains.
- Add psyllium fiber, 1 tablespoon a day in water. Start slowly.
- Walk every day.
- Go when you feel the urge. Put your feet on a stool.

Medicine that is safe in pregnancy:

- Polyethylene glycol, 17 grams in 8 ounces of liquid, once a day.
- For a few days only, if needed: senna or bisacodyl at bedtime.
- Do not use mineral oil, castor oil, or enemas unless we tell you to.

If you take iron, ask us about taking it every other day.

Call the clinic if you have no stool in 4 days with medicine, or blood in your stool.

Go to L&D if you have belly pain that comes and goes regularly, bleeding, or leaking fluid.

title: Recovery after vaginal birth
usage: Use as postpartum instructions after a vaginal delivery.
cerner_text:
Recovery after vaginal birth

Bleeding:

- Days 1 to 4: bright red, like a heavy period
- Days 5 to 10: pink or brown, lighter
- After that: yellow or white, light. It can last 4 to 6 weeks.
- Use pads only. Nothing in the vagina until we say it is OK.

Care of your bottom:

- Use a squirt bottle of warm water after each time you pee. Pat dry front to back.
- Use ice packs the first day, then warm sitz baths 2 to 3 times a day.
- Witch hazel pads help swelling and hemorrhoids.

Pain:

- Ibuprofen 600 mg by mouth every 6 hours
- Acetaminophen 650 mg by mouth every 6 hours
- Take them on a schedule for the first few days. Both are safe with breastfeeding.

Bowels: drink water, eat fiber, and walk. Ask about polyethylene glycol if you are constipated.

Your postpartum visit: _

Call the clinic if you have:

- Fever of 100.4 F or higher
- Bad-smelling discharge
- Bleeding that turns bright red again after it got lighter
- Trouble peeing
- Red, swollen, or warm leg
- Sad or anxious feelings most of the day

Go to the ER or call 911 if you have:

- Bleeding that soaks 1 pad an hour for 2 hours, or clots bigger than a golf ball
- Chest pain or trouble breathing
- A bad headache, vision changes, or a seizure
- Thoughts of hurting yourself or your baby

Incision care:

- You can shower. Let soapy water run over the incision and pat it dry.
- No baths, pools, or hot tubs until it is healed.
- Keep it dry. Tuck a clean cloth under your belly fold if needed.

- Walk several times a day. It helps prevent blood clots.
- Do not lift anything heavier than your baby for 6 weeks.
- Do not drive while taking opioid pain medicine, or until you can brake hard without pain.
- Hold a pillow on your belly when you cough or laugh.

Pain:

- Ibuprofen 600 mg by mouth every 6 hours
- Acetaminophen 650 mg by mouth every 6 hours
- Other pain medicine: _

Bleeding is normal for 4 to 6 weeks. Use pads only.

- Fever of 100.4 F or higher
- Redness spreading from the incision, or pus or drainage

- Pain that gets worse, not better

title: Mood after birth
usage: Use as postpartum instructions about baby blues, postpartum depression, and psychosis.
cerner_text:
Mood after birth

Baby blues:

- Up to 8 in 10 new mothers have tearfulness, mood swings, and worry in the first week.
- This goes away within 2 weeks.

Postpartum depression:

- About 1 in 8 mothers get it. It is a medical illness, not a sign that you are a bad mother.
- Signs: sadness most of the day, or trouble bonding with your baby.
- Other signs: bad anxiety or panic, not sleeping when your baby sleeps, or losing interest in things.
- Feeling numb or not bonded with your baby for more than 2 weeks can be a sign.
- It is treated with counseling, support, and medicine. Many medicines are safe with breastfeeding.
- Do not wait for your 6-week visit. Tell us now.

Postpartum anxiety:

- Constant worry about your baby, checking over and over, and a racing heart.
- This is common and treatable too.

Call or text the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline any time: 1-833-TLC-MAMA, which is 1-833-852-6262.

Call the clinic if signs last more than 2 weeks or are getting worse.

Call 911 or go to the ER right away if you:

- See or hear things that are not there
- Feel very confused or out of control
- Have thoughts of hurting yourself or your baby

You can also call or text 988.

title: Exercise after birth
usage: Use as postpartum instructions about returning to exercise.
cerner_text:
Exercise after birth

First days:

- Start Kegels when you are comfortable. Squeeze your pelvic floor for 3 to 5 seconds, then relax. Do 10 squeezes, 3 times a day.
- Take short walks.
- Practice deep belly breathing.

Weeks 2 to 6:

- Walk longer and faster as you feel ready.
- Gentle stretching is fine.
- Avoid sit-ups, crunches, planks, heavy lifting, and jumping.
- If you have more pain, bleeding, or pressure in your pelvis, slow down.

After your 6-week visit:

- Return to your usual exercise slowly. Start at half your usual effort.

- Leaking urine
- Pain with sex
- A bulge in the vagina
- A gap in the belly muscles

Ask us for a referral.

title: Birth control after birth
usage: Use as postpartum instructions about contraception after delivery.
cerner_text:
Birth control after birth

You can get pregnant as early as 3 weeks after birth, even before your period comes back. Waiting at least 18 months before your next pregnancy is healthiest for most people.

Can start any time, including right after birth:

- IUD
- Implant in the arm
- Shot every 3 months
- Progestin-only pill
- Condoms

Usually started 4 to 6 weeks after birth:

- Pill, patch, or ring with estrogen. Estrogen can raise the risk of blood clots right after birth.

Breastfeeding as birth control works only if all 3 are true:

- Your baby is under 6 months old
- Your period has not come back
- You feed only breast milk, at least every 4 hours in the day and every 6 hours at night

Permanent options: tubal surgery for you, or vasectomy for your partner.

Emergency birth control works best within 5 days after sex.

Your plan: _

Call the clinic to start or change birth control.

title: Breastfeeding basics
usage: Use as instructions for getting started with breastfeeding.
cerner_text:
Breastfeeding basics

Breastfeeding takes practice. Most problems can be fixed with help.

First days:

- Your first milk is thick and yellow. It comes in small amounts. This is exactly what your baby needs.
- More milk comes in on days 2 to 5.

A good latch:

- Your baby's mouth covers most of the dark area, not just the nipple.
- Both lips turn outward.
- You hear swallowing, not clicking.
- It should not hurt after the first 30 seconds. If it hurts, break the suction with a clean finger and try again.

Feed 8 to 12 times a day. Watch your baby, not the clock. Signs of hunger are rooting, hands to the mouth, and sucking.

Your baby is getting enough if:

- By day 5, at least 6 wet diapers and 3 to 4 yellow stools a day
- Your baby is back to birth weight by 2 weeks
- Your baby seems content after feeds

Lactation help: _

Call your baby's doctor if your baby:

- Has fewer wet diapers
- Is very sleepy and hard to wake for feeds
- Looks more yellow

title: Breastfeeding problems
usage: Use as instructions for common breastfeeding problems.
cerner_text:
Breastfeeding problems

Sore nipples:

- Check the latch first. This is the most common cause.
- Rub a little breast milk on your nipples after feeds and let them air dry.

Engorgement, when breasts are hard and full:

- Feed or pump every 2 to 3 hours.
- Use cold packs after feeds to bring down swelling.

Plugged duct or breast swelling:

- Keep feeding as usual. Do not pump extra to empty the breast.
- Use ice and take ibuprofen for pain and swelling.
- Use only light, gentle massage. Deep massage and heat can make it worse.

Low supply worries:

- The more your baby feeds, the more milk you make.
- Most people who worry about supply have enough.

Pumping: most insurance covers a breast pump. Milk keeps 4 days in the fridge and 6 to 12 months in the freezer.

Using formula is not failure. A fed baby is what matters most.

Call the clinic if you have:

- Fever of 100.4 F or higher with a red, painful area on your breast
- Flu-like aches with breast pain
- Burning nipple pain during and after feeds
- Cracked or bleeding nipples that do not heal

title: Formula feeding
usage: Use as instructions for formula feeding.
cerner_text:
Formula feeding

Formula is safe and complete food for your baby.

Choosing formula:

- Regular iron-fortified formula is right for most babies.
- Store brands are just as good as name brands.
- Do not switch formulas often for normal fussiness. Ask us first.

Making formula:

- Follow the package directions exactly.
- Use safe drinking water. For babies under 2 months, boil the water and let it cool.
- Warm the bottle in a bowl of warm water. Never use a microwave.

How much:

- Newborn: 1 to 2 ounces every 2 to 3 hours
- 2 months: 3 to 4 ounces every 3 to 4 hours
- 4 months: 4 to 6 ounces every 4 hours
- Feed when your baby is hungry. These are guides.

Storage:

- Throw away formula left in a bottle 1 hour after the feed starts.
- Mixed formula not yet used can stay in the fridge for 24 hours.

Never:

- Add water to make formula last longer
- Add cereal to a bottle
- Give cow's milk before 12 months

Call your baby's doctor if your baby vomits often, has fewer wet diapers, or has blood in the stool.

title: Safe sleep
usage: Use as instructions for safe infant sleep.
cerner_text:
Safe sleep for your baby

Follow the ABCs every sleep, with every caregiver.

- Alone: your baby sleeps alone, not with adults, children, or pets.
- Back: always put your baby on the back to sleep.
- Crib: use a firm, flat crib, bassinet, or play yard with only a fitted sheet.

Keep the sleep space empty:

- No pillows, blankets, bumpers, toys, or positioners.
- Dress your baby in a sleep sack instead of using a blanket.

More tips:

- Share a room with your baby for at least 6 months, but not a bed.
- Offer a pacifier at sleep time once breastfeeding is going well.
- Keep your baby from getting too hot.
- Keep your home and car smoke-free.
- Do not let your baby sleep in a swing, bouncer, or car seat outside the car.

Tummy time: when your baby is awake and someone is watching, place your baby on the tummy. Do this a few minutes, several times a day.

Call your baby's doctor with questions about sleep.

Call 911 if your baby is not breathing, turns blue, or is limp.

title: Cord care
usage: Use as instructions for umbilical cord care.
cerner_text:
Cord care

The cord stump dries up and falls off in 1 to 3 weeks.

What to do:

- Keep it clean and dry.
- Give sponge baths until it falls off.
- Fold the diaper down below the stump.
- You do not need alcohol wipes.
- Do not pull it off, even if it is barely hanging on.

Normal:

- It turns brown, then black, as it dries.
- A few drops of dried blood or a little clear fluid at the base
- A mild smell as it dries

Call your baby's doctor if:

- Redness spreads onto the skin around it
- It has a bad smell or yellow or green pus
- It bleeds and does not stop with gentle pressure
- It has not fallen off by 3 weeks

Go to the ER if your baby has a fever of 100.4 F or higher.

Jaundice makes the skin and eyes look yellow. About 6 in 10 babies get it in the first week. Most cases are mild and go away on their own.

- Feed often, at least 8 to 12 times a day.
- Do not put your baby in the sun to treat it. It does not work well and can burn.

title: Normal newborn things
usage: Use as instructions about normal newborn findings that worry parents.
cerner_text:
Normal newborn things

These are normal and go away on their own:

- Cone-shaped head after birth
- Soft spots on the head that pulse
- White, cheesy coating on the skin
- Fine hair on the back and shoulders
- Swollen breasts, in boys or girls
- Swollen labia or scrotum
- A little blood or mucus from the vagina in baby girls
- Eyes that cross sometimes, until about 4 months
- Peeling skin
- Lots of sneezing and hiccups
- A rash of small red spots with white centers in the first days
- Black, sticky first stools in the first 2 days

Call your baby's doctor right away if your baby:

- Has a fever of 100.4 F or higher. Take the temperature in the bottom.
- Will not eat
- Looks very yellow
- Grunts with every breath
- Has very pale skin
- Cannot be calmed
- Has fewer than 6 wet diapers a day after day 5

Fever in the first 3 months is an emergency. Go to the ER.

Call 911 if your baby has blue or gray lips or face.

Vitamin D drops for your baby

Breast milk is low in vitamin D. Vitamin D helps your baby build strong bones.

Who needs drops:

- Every baby who drinks breast milk, even with some formula
- Start in the first few days of life.
- Babies who drink enough formula, about 32 ounces a day, do not need drops.

Your baby's dose: _

How to give it:

- Read the label. Products are different strengths. More is not better.
- Put the drop on your nipple before a feed, or on a clean finger your baby is sucking.

Call your baby's doctor with questions about vitamin D or if your baby stops feeding well.

title: Car seat safety
usage: Use as instructions about infant car seat safety.
cerner_text:
Car seat safety

You need a car seat to take your baby home from the hospital.

How to use it:

- Rear-facing, in the back seat, as long as your seat allows. This is usually past age 2.
- Never in front of an airbag.
- Straps at or below the shoulders.
- Straps tight enough that you cannot pinch extra strap at the shoulder.
- Chest clip at armpit level.
- No bulky coats under the straps. Buckle your baby in, then put a blanket over the top.
- Do not add padding or inserts that did not come with the seat.
- Do not use a seat that has been in a crash or is past its expiration date.

Get the install checked for free at many fire stations or hospitals, before your due date.

Call your baby's doctor with car seat questions.

title: Circumcision care
usage: Use as instructions after newborn circumcision or for care of the uncircumcised penis.
cerner_text:
Penis care

If your baby was circumcised:

- Put petroleum jelly on the tip with every diaper change for about 1 week.
- A yellow crust is normal. Do not wipe it off.
- If a plastic ring was used, it falls off on its own in 5 to 8 days. Do not pull it.
- Clean gently with warm water only.

If your baby is not circumcised:

- Do not pull back the foreskin. It separates on its own over several years.
- Wash the outside like any other skin.

Call your baby's doctor if:

- Bleeding is more than a few drops, or a spot bigger than a quarter
- Your baby has no wet diaper in 8 hours
- Redness or swelling spreads, or there is pus
- The plastic ring has not fallen off in 10 days

Go to the ER if your baby has a fever of 100.4 F or higher.

title: Crying and coping
usage: Use as instructions about normal infant crying and never shaking a baby.
cerner_text:
Crying and coping

All babies cry. Crying often gets worse around 2 weeks and peaks around 6 to 8 weeks. It gets better by 3 to 4 months. Some babies cry for hours, even when nothing is wrong.

Try:

- Feeding or burping
- A clean diaper
- Swaddling, only until your baby starts to roll
- Holding your baby on the side while awake, rocking, or swaying
- Shushing sounds or white noise
- A walk in the stroller or a car ride

If you feel angry or at your limit:

- Put your baby on the back in the crib.
- Leave the room and close the door.
- Take 10 minutes to calm down. Call someone you trust.
- It is OK to let your baby cry while you calm down.

Never shake a baby. Shaking can cause brain damage or death. Make sure everyone who cares for your baby knows this.

Call your baby's doctor if crying comes with fever, vomiting, poor feeding, or your baby seems in pain.

Call 911 if your baby is limp, hard to wake, or has trouble breathing.

- Discharge with preterm labor precautions
- OB follow-up in 1 week

title: Delirium prevention orders
usage: Use as the plan or nursing communication for delirium prevention in hospitalized patients.
cerner_text:
Delirium prevention orders

- CAM screen every shift
- Awake with lights and TV on during the day, lights off 2200 to 0600
- Glasses and hearing aids on and working
- Reorient often, family at bedside encouraged
- Cluster overnight care, no vitals, labs, or baths 2300 to 0600 unless needed for safety
- Up to chair for meals, out of bed and walking as able, PT and OT consult
- Remove unneeded lines, restraints, and Foley, bladder scan every 8 hours if not voiding, straight cath for retention
- Avoid anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, and sedative hypnotics, no scheduled opioids unless needed for pain
- Acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours scheduled for pain _
- Melatonin 3 mg PO nightly as the only sleep aid
- Bowel regimen, hydration, glucose control
- Delirium precautions sign on door

- SpO2 goal 88 to 92 percent, awake and asleep
- Brief dips to 88 percent during sleep are expected, do not increase oxygen for them
- Increase oxygen only for SpO2 under 88 percent for 5 minutes or longer, or repeated drops under 88 percent despite current oxygen
- Wean oxygen if SpO2 stays above 92 percent, to limit CO2 retention
- Page the physician before increasing oxygen flow
- Page for new confusion, drowsiness, or increased work of breathing

title: High blood pressure
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for hypertension.
cerner_text:
High blood pressure

Your blood pressure goal is below 130 over 80.

High blood pressure can hurt your heart, brain, and kidneys. Most people do not feel it.

What you can do:

- Take your medicine every day, even if you feel fine.
- Eat more fruits, vegetables, beans, and whole grains.
- Use less salt. Aim for less than 2,300 mg of sodium a day. Less than 1,500 mg is even better.
- Read food labels. Canned, frozen, and restaurant foods have a lot of salt.
- Be active for 30 minutes on most days.
- Limit alcohol. Do not smoke.
- Check your blood pressure at home and write it down. Bring your log to every visit.

Call the clinic if your blood pressure is over 160 over 100 more than once.

Call 911 or go to the ER if your blood pressure is over 180 over 120 and you have:

- Chest pain
- Trouble breathing
- A bad headache
- Weakness or trouble speaking
- Vision changes

title: Diabetes
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for diabetes.
cerner_text:
Diabetes

Your blood sugar goal before meals is 80 to 130. Your A1c goal is _.

Plate method for meals:

- Fill half your plate with vegetables.
- Fill one quarter with lean protein like chicken, fish, beans, or eggs.
- Fill one quarter with starch like brown rice, potatoes, or whole grain bread.
- Drink water instead of soda or juice.

Be active for 30 minutes on 5 days each week.

Low blood sugar is below 70. Signs are shaking, sweating, fast heartbeat, hunger, confusion, or feeling dizzy. If this happens, eat or drink 15 grams of sugar, like 4 ounces of juice or 4 glucose tablets. Check again in 15 minutes. Repeat if still below 70.

Foot care:

- Look at your feet every day for cuts, blisters, or color changes.
- Wear shoes and socks. Do not walk barefoot.
- Keep your feet clean and dry.

Get a diabetes eye exam every year.

Call the clinic if your sugar is often over 250 or under 70. Go to the ER if you are confused, vomiting and cannot keep fluids down, or very short of breath.

title: Home blood pressure
usage: Use as instructions for checking blood pressure at home.
cerner_text:
How to check your blood pressure at home

- Use an arm cuff that fits your upper arm.
- Do not smoke, exercise, or drink coffee for 30 minutes before.
- Empty your bladder.
- Sit in a chair with your back supported and feet flat on the floor. Do not cross your legs.
- Rest quietly for 5 minutes.
- Put your arm on a table at the level of your heart.
- Put the cuff on bare skin.
- Do not talk during the reading.
- Take 2 readings 1 minute apart. Write both down.
- Check in the morning and in the evening for 7 days before your next visit.

Bring your log and your cuff to your next visit.

Call 911 if your blood pressure is over 180 over 120 and you have:

- Chest pain
- Trouble breathing
- A bad headache
- Weakness
- Vision changes

title: Low back pain
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for acute low back pain.
cerner_text:
Low back pain

Most back pain gets better in 4 to 6 weeks. X-rays and scans are usually not needed.

What helps:

- Keep moving. Walk a little more each day.
- Avoid bed rest. It can make pain last longer.
- Use heat for 15 to 20 minutes at a time.
- Take your pain medicine as directed.
- Do the stretches you were shown.

Go to the ER right away if you have:

- New weakness or numbness in your legs
- Trouble controlling your bladder or bowels
- Numbness in your groin or inner thighs
- Fever with back pain
- Back pain after a bad fall or accident

Call the clinic if your pain is not better in 4 weeks or gets worse.

title: Cold and upper respiratory infection
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for a viral upper respiratory infection.
cerner_text:
Colds and upper respiratory infections

Colds are caused by viruses. Antibiotics do not help.

Most people feel better in about 1 week. A cough can last 2 to 3 weeks.

What helps:

- Rest and drink plenty of fluids.
- Use saline nose spray or a humidifier.
- Honey can help a cough. Do not give honey to babies under 1 year old.
- Use acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever or pain as directed on the label. For children, use the dose based on weight.
- Wash your hands often. Cover your cough.

Call the clinic if:

- Fever lasts more than 3 days
- Symptoms last more than 10 days or get better and then worse
- You have bad ear pain or sinus pain

Go to the ER if you have:

- Trouble breathing or chest pain
- Lips turning blue
- Confusion
- Signs of dehydration, like no urine in 8 hours

- Drink warm or cold liquids.

title: Sprain

Sprain

- Raise it above the level of your heart.

After 2 to 3 days:

- Start moving it gently.
- Slowly return to normal activity as pain allows.

Use acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed on the label.

Call the clinic if you cannot put weight on it after 1 week or it is not getting better.

- Your fingers or toes are numb, cold, pale, or blue
- You have very bad pain

title: Concussion
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for concussion.
cerner_text:
Concussion

A concussion is a mild brain injury. Common symptoms are headache, dizziness, feeling tired, and trouble focusing. Most people feel better in 2 to 4 weeks.

First 1 to 2 days:

- Rest, but you do not need to stay in a dark room.
- Limit screens, reading, and loud places if they make symptoms worse.
- Do not drink alcohol.
- Use acetaminophen for headache.

After that:

- Slowly add light activity like walking, as long as symptoms do not get worse.
- Go back to school or work with breaks as needed. School or work note: _
- Do not drive until _.
- Sleep at regular times.

No sports, contact activities, or anything that could cause another head injury until a doctor clears you. Return to sports step by step.

Call the clinic if you are not getting better in 2 weeks or symptoms get worse.

Go to the ER right away if you have:

- A headache that gets worse and worse
- Vomiting more than once
- A seizure
- Trouble waking up, or being very sleepy
- Confusion, slurred speech, or acting strange
- Weakness or numbness
- One pupil larger than the other

title: Constipation
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for constipation.
cerner_text:
Constipation

Constipation means hard stools or not going often. It is common and usually gets better with simple changes.

What helps:

- Eat more fiber, like fruit, vegetables, beans, and whole grains. Add it slowly.
- Drink 8 to 10 cups of fluid a day, mostly water.
- Move your body every day.
- Sit on the toilet at the same time each day, like after breakfast.
- Put your feet on a small stool when you sit on the toilet.
- Do not ignore the urge to go.

Medicine: polyethylene glycol 17 grams mixed in 8 ounces of liquid by mouth once a day. Use less if stools get too loose.

Call the clinic if:

- You have not had a stool in 3 days, even with medicine
- You see blood in your stool
- You lose weight without trying

Go to the ER if you have bad belly pain, a swollen belly with vomiting, or cannot pass gas.

title: Fever in children
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for fever in children.
cerner_text:
Fever in children

A fever is a temperature of 100.4 F or higher. Fever helps the body fight infection. It is not dangerous by itself.

Treat your child's comfort, not the number. How your child acts matters more than the temperature.

Fever does not cause brain damage. It often comes back when medicine wears off. Fevers from viruses usually last 2 to 3 days.

What helps:

- Give plenty of fluids.
- Dress your child in light clothes.
- Let your child rest.

Fever medicine:

- Acetaminophen: 15 mg/kg by mouth every 4 to 6 hours as needed. No more than 5 doses in 24 hours. Max 75 mg/kg a day, and never more than 4,000 mg a day.
- Ibuprofen: only for age 6 months and older. 10 mg/kg by mouth every 6 to 8 hours as needed. Max 40 mg/kg a day, and never more than 400 mg per dose.
- Your child's weight: _ kg
- Your child's acetaminophen dose: _ mL of _
- Your child's ibuprofen dose: _ mL of _
- Never give aspirin to children.

Babies under 3 months: a fever of 100.4 F or higher means go to the ER now. Do not give medicine first.

Call the clinic if:

- Fever lasts more than 24 hours in a child under 2 years
- Fever lasts more than 3 days in an older child
- Your child has ear pain, a sore throat, or pain when peeing
- Your child has fewer wet diapers or is peeing less

Go to the ER or call 911 if your child:

- Has trouble breathing
- Is hard to wake up or very floppy
- Cannot be calmed down
- Has a rash of purple spots that do not fade when pressed
- Has a stiff neck or a seizure
- Has not peed in 8 hours

title: Vomiting and diarrhea in children
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for pediatric gastroenteritis.
cerner_text:
Vomiting and diarrhea in children

This is usually caused by a virus. Vomiting often stops in 1 to 2 days. Loose stools can last 1 to 2 weeks. The most important thing is to keep your child from getting dried out.

Give fluids:

- Use oral rehydration solution from the store.
- Give 1 teaspoon, or 5 mL, every 5 minutes with a spoon or syringe.
- If your child vomits, wait 15 minutes and start again.
- Slowly give more as your child keeps it down.
- If you breastfeed, keep nursing. Feed more often for shorter times.
- Avoid juice, soda, and sports drinks. They can make diarrhea worse.

Go back to normal food once vomiting stops.

Nausea medicine: _

Wash hands often, especially after diaper changes.

Signs your child is dried out:

- No pee or wet diaper in 8 hours
- Dry mouth or no tears when crying
- Sunken eyes
- Very sleepy or fussy

Call the clinic if vomiting lasts more than 24 hours or diarrhea lasts more than 1 week.

Go to the ER if your child has:

- Signs of being dried out
- Green or bloody vomit
- Blood in the stool
- Bad belly pain
- Trouble waking up

usage: Use as after-visit instructions for croup.
cerner_text:
Croup

Croup is caused by a virus. It swells the airway below the voice box. It causes a barky cough, a hoarse voice, and noisy breathing. It is often worse at night. It usually lasts 3 to 5 days.

Your child got a steroid medicine today: _

What helps:

- Keep your child calm. Crying makes breathing harder.
- Hold and comfort your child.
- Cool night air may help some children.
- Give plenty of fluids.
- For fever, use acetaminophen or ibuprofen. See our fever handout for your child's dose.
- Do not smoke around your child.

Call the clinic if croup lasts more than 1 week or fever lasts more than 3 days.

Call 911 or go to the ER if your child:

- Is working hard to breathe, or the skin pulls in between the ribs
- Has noisy breathing when calm and resting
- Is drooling or cannot swallow
- Has blue or gray lips
- Is very sleepy or hard to wake
epic_text:
Croup

Croup is caused by a virus. It swells the airway below the voice box. It causes a barky cough, a hoarse voice, and noisy breathing. It is often worse at night. It usually lasts 3 to 5 days.

Your child got a steroid medicine today: ***

What helps:

- Keep your child calm. Crying makes breathing harder.
- Hold and comfort your child.
- Cool night air may help some children.
- Give plenty of fluids.
- For fever, use acetaminophen or ibuprofen. See our fever handout for your child's dose.
- Do not smoke around your child.

Call the clinic if croup lasts more than 1 week or fever lasts more than 3 days.

Call 911 or go to the ER if your child:

- Is working hard to breathe, or the skin pulls in between the ribs
- Has noisy breathing when calm and resting
- Is drooling or cannot swallow
- Has blue or gray lips
- Is very sleepy or hard to wake

title: Bronchiolitis
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for bronchiolitis in infants and toddlers.
cerner_text:
Bronchiolitis

Bronchiolitis is a virus that causes swelling in the small airways of the lungs. It is common in babies and children under 2. It causes a runny nose, cough, and wheezing.

It is usually worst on days 3 to 5. The cough can last 2 to 4 weeks. Antibiotics do not help.

What helps:

- Put salt water drops in the nose and use a bulb suction before feeding and sleep.
- Give smaller feedings more often.
- Keep your child away from smoke.
- Wash hands often. Keep your child away from young babies.

Call the clinic if:

- Your child is drinking less than half the usual amount
- Fever lasts more than 3 days
- Your child has ear pain

Call 911 or go to the ER if your child:

- Is breathing very fast or working hard to breathe
- Has skin pulling in between the ribs, grunting, or flaring nostrils
- Stops breathing for a few seconds
- Has blue or gray lips
- Has not had a wet diaper in 8 hours
- Is under 3 months old with a fever of 100.4 F or higher

title: Newborn care
usage: Use as after-visit instructions at newborn and early well visits.
cerner_text:
Caring for your newborn

Feeding:

- Breastfed babies eat 8 to 12 times a day.
- Formula: about _ ounces every 2 to 3 hours.
- Wake your baby to eat if it has been 3 hours during the day or 4 hours at night.
- Ask us about vitamin D drops: _

Diapers:

- By day 5, expect at least 6 wet diapers a day.
- Stools turn yellow and seedy by day 5 for breastfed babies.

Sleep safety:

- Always put your baby to sleep on the back.
- Use a crib or bassinet with a firm, flat mattress.
- No blankets, pillows, bumpers, or toys in the crib.
- Share a room, but not a bed.

Other care:

- Keep the cord dry. It falls off in 1 to 3 weeks.
- Use a rear-facing car seat every ride.
- Keep your home and car smoke-free.
- Never shake a baby. If crying is too much, put your baby in the crib and step away for a few minutes.
- Parents can have depression after a baby. Tell us if you feel sad or hopeless.

Call the clinic if your baby:

- Has yellow skin spreading to the belly or legs
- Is very sleepy or not feeding well
- Has fewer wet diapers than expected
- Has a red or bad-smelling cord
- Vomits green

Call 911 if your baby has trouble breathing, turns blue, is limp, or will not wake up.

Next visit: _

title: Iron pills
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for iron deficiency anemia.
cerner_text:
Iron pills

Your iron is low. Iron helps your blood carry oxygen. Low iron can make you tired, short of breath, or dizzy.

How to take iron:

- Take _ by mouth _.
- Taking it every other day works as well and causes less stomach upset.
- Take it with water or orange juice, 1 hour before a meal if you can.
- If it upsets your stomach, take it with a small snack.
- Take it 2 hours apart from antacids, calcium, dairy, tea, and coffee.

What to expect:

- Your stools will turn dark green or black. This is normal.
- Constipation is common. Drink water and eat fiber.
- You will need iron for about 3 months after your blood count is normal.

Keep iron pills away from children. Too much iron can be deadly for a child.

Blood test again on _.

Call the clinic if you cannot take the pills because of side effects.

Go to the ER if you have:

- Black, sticky stools with dizziness
- Vomiting blood
- Chest pain or trouble breathing

title: Gout
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for gout.
cerner_text:
Gout

Gout happens when uric acid builds up and forms crystals in a joint. It causes sudden pain, redness, and swelling.

During a flare:

- Take _ as soon as the flare starts.
- Rest and raise the joint. Use ice for 20 minutes at a time.
- Drink plenty of water.

To prevent flares:

- Take _ every day, even when you feel fine.
- Flares can happen in the first few months on this medicine. Keep taking it.
- Limit beer, liquor, red meat, organ meats, and shellfish.
- Avoid soda and drinks with high fructose corn syrup.
- Lose weight slowly if you are overweight.

Uric acid blood test on _.

Call the clinic if a flare does not improve in 3 days, or you get a rash on allopurinol.

Go to the ER if the joint is red and hot and you have a fever or chills.

cerner_text:
Bone health

Osteoporosis means your bones are thin and break easily. Treatment lowers your risk of a broken bone.

What you can do:

- Get calcium from food, like milk, yogurt, cheese, and leafy greens.
- Take vitamin D every day: _
- Walk and do strength exercises most days.
- Do not smoke. Limit alcohol.
- Prevent falls. Remove rugs, add night lights, and use rails.

If you take alendronate:

- Take it once a week, first thing in the morning.
- Swallow it with a full glass of plain water.
- Stay sitting or standing for 30 minutes.
- Do not eat, drink, or take other pills for 30 minutes.
- See your dentist regularly.

Bone scan again in _.

Call the clinic if you have heartburn or pain when swallowing on alendronate, or new thigh or groin pain.

Go to the ER if you fall and cannot stand, or have severe pain after a fall.

usage: Use as after-visit instructions for allergic rhinitis.
cerner_text:
Nose allergies

Allergies cause a runny or stuffy nose, sneezing, and itchy eyes.

What helps:

- Use your steroid nose spray every day. It works best after 1 to 2 weeks.
- Point the spray toward the outside of your nose, away from the middle.
- Take an allergy pill like cetirizine or loratadine when needed.
- Rinse your nose with salt water. Use distilled or boiled water that has cooled.
- Keep windows closed on high pollen days.
- Shower and change clothes after being outside.
- Wash bedding in hot water each week.

Call the clinic if you have nosebleeds, symptoms do not get better in 4 weeks, or you have wheezing.

Eczema is dry, itchy skin that comes and goes. It is not contagious.

Daily skin care:

- Use a thick, fragrance-free cream or ointment at least 2 times a day.
- Put it on within 3 minutes after a bath.
- Take short baths or showers in lukewarm water.
- Use a gentle, fragrance-free soap.
- Pat skin dry. Do not rub.

During a flare:

- Use _ on red, itchy areas _ times a day for up to _ days.
- Then go back to moisturizer only.
- Keep nails short. Try not to scratch.

Avoid wool, scented products, and very hot or dry air.

Call the clinic if the skin is not better in 2 weeks, or you have yellow crusts, pus, or pain.

Go to the ER if you have painful blisters or sores with fever.

- Morning: wash with benzoyl peroxide wash. It can bleach towels and clothes.
- Night: put a pea-sized amount of _ on your whole face, not just on pimples.

title: Fall prevention
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for fall prevention in older adults.
cerner_text:
Preventing falls

Falls are common but many can be prevented.

At home:

- Remove loose rugs and clutter from floors.
- Add night lights in halls, bedrooms, and bathrooms.
- Put grab bars in the shower and by the toilet.
- Use rails on both sides of stairs.
- Keep things you use often within easy reach.

Your body:

- Do the balance and strength exercises you were shown.
- Stand up slowly. Sit on the edge of the bed for a minute first.
- Wear shoes with thin, non-slip soles inside and outside.
- Use your cane or walker every time: _
- Get your eyes checked every year.

Medicines: we changed _. Ask us before taking sleep aids or allergy pills.

Call the clinic if you fall, even if you are not hurt.

Call 911 if you:

- Fall and cannot get up
- Hit your head while on a blood thinner
- Have new weakness or confusion

title: Constipation in children
usage: Use as after-visit instructions for functional constipation in children.
cerner_text:
Constipation in children

Constipation is common in children. Hard stools hurt, so children hold them in. This makes it worse. Treatment breaks this cycle.

Medicine:

- Polyethylene glycol powder, mixed in 4 to 8 ounces of drink.
- Your child's dose: _ capfuls or _ grams, _ times a day.
- Goal: 1 to 2 soft stools every day.
- If stools are watery, use less. If stools are still hard, use more.
- Keep giving it for at least 2 months, even when things get better. Stopping too soon often brings it back.

Toilet time:

- Have your child sit on the toilet for 5 minutes after meals.
- Use a footstool so knees are higher than hips.
- Praise trying. Never punish accidents.

Food and drink:

- Offer fruits, vegetables, beans, and whole grains.
- Give plenty of water.
- Limit milk to 2 to 3 cups a day.

Call the clinic if your child has:

- Belly pain that does not go away
- Blood in the stool
- No stool in 3 days on medicine

Go to the ER if your child has a swollen belly with vomiting, green vomit, or severe belly pain.

title: About benzodiazepines
usage: Use as patient education for long-term benzodiazepine or Z-drug use.
cerner_text:
Your benzodiazepine medicine

Your medicine: _

Benzodiazepines include alprazolam, clonazepam, lorazepam, diazepam, and temazepam. Sleep pills like zolpidem work in a similar way.

They can help for a short time. Used for months or years, they can cause:

- Falls and broken hips
- Memory and thinking problems
- Car crashes
- Daytime sleepiness
- Breathing problems, especially with opioids or alcohol

Over time, your body gets used to the medicine. It may stop helping sleep or worry as much. Stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal, including seizures.

The good news:

- Most people can lower or stop their dose with a slow plan.
- We go slowly and can pause any time.
- Counseling and some daily medicines work well for worry and sleep.

Do not stop or change your dose on your own. Talk with us first.

Call the clinic if you have questions or want to start a plan.

Call 911 if someone has a seizure, severe confusion, or trouble breathing.

title: Screen time for kids

Screen time for kids

Under 18 months: avoid screens except video chats with family.
18 to 24 months: if you use screens, pick good shows or apps. Watch with your child.
Ages 2 to 5: limit screens to 1 hour a day of good shows. Watch together and talk about what you see.
Ages 6 and up: make a family media plan. Set limits on time and type of media.

Turn screens off 1 hour before bed.
Do not use screens during meals.

Call us if your child has trouble sleeping, gets very upset when screens end, or seems sad or withdrawn.

title: Summer safety for kids
usage: Use for summer anticipatory guidance at child visits.
cerner_text:
Summer safety for kids

Wear a helmet for bikes, scooters, skates, and skateboards.
Watch your child closely around any water, including bathtubs, pools, lakes, and splash pads.
Stay within arm's reach of young children in water.
Use sunscreen SPF 30 or higher. Put it on again every 2 hours and after swimming.
Keep babies under 6 months out of direct sun.
Use bug spray with DEET or picaridin to prevent tick and mosquito bites. Do not use it on babies under 2 months.
Check for ticks after time outside.
Give lots of water on hot days.
Never leave a child alone in a car.

Call us if your child has a rash or fever after a tick bite.

Call 911 if your child stops breathing, is pulled from the water, or is hot and confused.

title: Piriformis stretch
usage: Use to give a patient home piriformis stretch instructions.
cerner_text:
Piriformis stretch

Lie on your back with both knees bent.
Cross one ankle over the other knee.
Hold the outside of the bent knee with the opposite hand.
Gently pull that knee toward the opposite shoulder until you feel a stretch in your buttock.
Breathe slowly and hold for 20 to 30 seconds.
Switch sides.
Do this 2 to 3 times on each side, 1 to 2 times a day.

Stop if the stretch causes sharp pain.

Call us if the pain lasts more than 6 weeks or spreads down your leg.

Go to the ER if you have new leg weakness, numbness between your legs, or trouble controlling urine or stool.

title: Healthy lifestyle choices
usage: Use as a handout for general heart-healthy lifestyle changes.
cerner_text:
Healthy choices can lower your risk of heart attack, stroke, kidney disease and memory loss.
They can also help your weight and your mood.
Pick 2 or 3 of these to start before your next visit:

- Eat a breakfast with protein, like eggs, yogurt or nuts
- Eat smaller portions at meals
- Cut back on sugary drinks, sweets, white bread and white rice
- Drink water instead of soda or juice
- Eat vegetables and fruits of different colors every day
- Cook with olive oil or canola oil instead of butter
- Eat fish 2 times a week
- Walk or move your body for 30 minutes, 5 days a week
- If you drink alcohol, drink less, and less is better
- If you smoke or vape, ask us for help to quit
- Use sunscreen when you are outside

Call us if you have questions or want help making a plan.
Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of stroke like face drooping or weakness on one side.

title: Low-dose buprenorphine initiation evidence
usage: Use as a physician reference on low-dose, or micro, buprenorphine initiation. Not for the chart.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Low-dose buprenorphine initiation

Small buprenorphine doses are started while the patient continues the full agonist, so withdrawal is not required. Also called microdosing or micro-induction.

When to consider:

- High risk of precipitated withdrawal, such as regular fentanyl use
- Prior precipitated withdrawal
- Patient cannot tolerate withdrawal, or has pain that needs ongoing full agonist
- Transition from methadone or high-dose full agonist

Evidence:

- Bernese method, 2 cases: start 0.2 mg with overlapping heroin use, small daily increases, then abrupt stop of the full agonist once at a sufficient dose. In case 2: day 1 0.2 mg, day 2 0.4 mg BID, then up 0.4 mg/day to 3.4 mg. Then up 20 to 30 percent per day, reaching 24 mg. The full agonist stopped on day 29.
- Review of 18 papers, 63 patients: start doses mostly 0.2 to 0.5 mg. Most transitions took 4 to 8 days and ended at 8 to 16 mg.
- Updated systematic review, 59 studies, 682 patients: 81 percent completed the transition, clinically significant withdrawal in 7 percent.
- Systematic review, 47 studies, 924 patients: successful rotation 96 percent with microdosing vs 95.6 percent with traditional initiation.
- Low-dose initiation in pregnancy, review of 25 patients: precipitated withdrawal in 8 percent.
- Evidence is mostly case series and observational. No schedule is proven best.

Principles: start low, titrate gradually, continue the full agonist until the target dose, and pause increases if withdrawal appears.

The $bupmicro 7-day schedule is a representative example within these published ranges, not a validated trial protocol. Patient schedule: $pibupmicro.

- Hammig R et al. Subst Abuse Rehabil 2016;7:99-105. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27499655/
- Ahmed S et al. Am J Addict 2021;30(4):305-315. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33378137/
- Cohen SM et al. J Addict Med 2022;16(4):399-406. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34954746/
- Adams KK et al. Addict Sci Clin Pract 2025;20:19. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39980050/
- Spreen LA et al. Pharmacotherapy 2022;42(5):411-427. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35302671/

title: Fentanyl and precipitated withdrawal
usage: Use as a physician reference on precipitated withdrawal risk and management. Not for the chart.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Fentanyl and precipitated withdrawal

Precipitated withdrawal is a rapid worsening of withdrawal right after buprenorphine. Buprenorphine displaces the full agonist but has lower intrinsic activity.

How often:

- 28 EDs, 1,200 patients, standard dosing of 8 mg if COWS 8 or more then 16 mg/day: precipitated withdrawal in 0.76 percent. All 9 cases were fentanyl positive.
- Hospitalized patients, 226 patients: 11.5 percent overall, 16.3 percent with confirmed fentanyl use. Higher risk with urine fentanyl 200 ng/mL or more, aOR 8.37, and BMI 30 or more, aOR 5.12.

Risk factors: chronic fentanyl use, methadone use, concurrent benzodiazepine use.

Prevention:

- Wait for moderate withdrawal, COWS over 13, and enough time since last full agonist use
- Or use a low-dose or high-dose strategy
- Individualize initiation, dose, and dosing frequency

Management:

- Additional buprenorphine has a pharmacologic basis and has worked in case reports
- Symptom-based adjuncts and support
- Most cases are benign, but patients may avoid buprenorphine afterward

Protocol phrase: $bupprecip.

Sources:

- D'Onofrio G et al. JAMA Netw Open 2023;6(3):e236108. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36995717/
- Thakrar AP et al. JAMA Netw Open 2024;7(9):e2435895. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39331392/
- Spadaro A et al. Am J Emerg Med 2022;58:22-26. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35623179/
- Weimer MB et al. ASAM Clinical Considerations, high-potency synthetic opioids. J Addict Med 2023;17(6):632-639. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37934520/

Complex persistent opioid dependence, CPOD

Definition:

- A gray zone between simple physical dependence and opioid use disorder in patients on long-term opioid therapy.
- Recognized as a desire to continue or increase the dose, or inability to stop despite a prescriber's recommendation to stop.
- Symptoms: worsening pain, function, mood, and sleep; escalating opioid need while on therapy; protracted withdrawal with dose reduction.
- The 2017 paper called it complex persistent dependence. The 2020 paper named it CPOD: clinically distinct from but biologically similar to OUD, and neither necessary nor sufficient for OUD.
- Suggested features: 100 MME/day or more and/or significant pain dysfunction, aberrancies or misuse, psychiatric burden, or a substance use history.

Why it matters:

- Tapering in 113,618 patients on 50 MME/day or more: overdose 9.3 vs 5.5 per 100 person-years, aIRR 1.68; mental health crisis 7.6 vs 3.3, aIRR 2.28. Each 10 percent faster monthly reduction raised both risks.
- VA cohort of 1.39 million: overdose or suicide death after stopping rose with treatment length, HR 6.77 after more than 400 days of treatment. Risk was highest right after stopping.

Options:

- Continue with risk reduction: naloxone, no benzodiazepines, PDMP, function goals.
- Slow taper with patient agreement: $opitaper, evidence in .edopitaper.
- Rotate to buprenorphine if unable to taper despite worsening pain or function, whether or not OUD criteria are met: $bupcpod. Review of 22 studies, 1,616 participants: very low-quality evidence that rotation maintained or improved analgesia with low risk of precipitated withdrawal; steady dosing better tolerated than tapered dosing.

title: Opioid tapering guidance
section: Physician education: opioids, benzodiazepines, and deprescribing
usage: Use as a physician reference on opioid taper rates and safety. Not for the chart.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Opioid tapering

Never abrupt:

- HHS: opioids should not be tapered rapidly or discontinued suddenly.
- CDC 2022: unless there is a life-threatening issue, do not stop abruptly or rapidly reduce from higher doses.
- FDA 2019: serious withdrawal, uncontrolled pain, psychological distress, and suicide reported after sudden discontinuation in dependent patients.

Rates:

- After 1 year or more of use: about 10 percent per month or slower, per HHS and CDC.
- After weeks to months of use: 10 percent of the original dose per week or slower. At 30 percent of the original dose, switch to 10 percent of the remaining dose per week.
- HHS: common tapers are 5 to 20 percent every 4 weeks.
- FDA: no more than 10 to 25 percent every 2 to 4 weeks.

Pauses:

- Tapers may be paused and restarted when the patient is ready, and may need to slow at low doses.
- Significant withdrawal may mean pausing or slowing.
- FDA: it may be necessary to return to the previous dose, then taper more gradually once stable.

If tapering fails or OUD emerges, consider buprenorphine: .edcpod.

Sources:

- HHS 2019 guide: https://www.hhs.gov/system/files/Dosage_Reduction_Discontinuation.pdf
- CDC 2022 guideline, Dowell D et al. MMWR Recomm Rep 2022;71(3):1-95. https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/71/rr/rr7103a1.htm
- FDA 2019 safety announcement: https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-identifies-harm-reported-sudden-discontinuation-opioid-pain-medicines-and-requires-label-changes

section: Physician education: opioids, benzodiazepines, and deprescribing
usage: Use as a physician reference on long-term benzodiazepine use, dependence, and when to taper. Not for the chart.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Long-term benzodiazepine use

Is there a benzodiazepine version of CPOD?

- No established term. The joint guideline uses physiologic dependence, distinct from sedative use disorder.
- BIND, benzodiazepine-induced neurological dysfunction, is a proposed term for symptoms during use, tapering, and after stopping. The evidence is a self-selected online survey of 1,207 people with no control group.

FDA 2020 boxed warning:

- Covers abuse, misuse, addiction, physical dependence, and withdrawal.
- Abrupt discontinuation or rapid reduction can cause life-threatening withdrawal.
- FDA 2016 warning: limit opioid plus benzodiazepine prescribing to patients without adequate alternatives.

Joint clinical practice guideline, 2025:

- Avoid abrupt discontinuation in patients likely to be physically dependent.
- Taper when risks outweigh benefits; reassess at least every 3 months.
- Generally taper in older adults unless there are compelling reasons to continue.
- Offer CBT or CBT-I alongside the taper.
- Rates and pauses: .edbzdtaper.

Older adults:

- Beers 2023: avoid benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older adults, with exceptions such as seizure disorders, REM sleep behavior disorder, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, and severe generalized anxiety.
- Deprescribing guideline: taper for adults 65 and older regardless of duration; suggested for ages 18 to 64 after more than 4 weeks of use.

Patients agree to taper when asked well:

- EMPOWER, 303 adults aged 65 to 95: direct-to-patient education. At 6 months, 27 percent discontinued vs 5 percent with usual care, NNT 4.
- D-PRESCRIBE: pharmacist-led education, sedative-hypnotics stopped in 43 vs 9 percent; no hospitalizations among those tapering.

Phrases: $bzd, #bzd, $bzdtaper, $bzdlet, $pibzd, $pibzdtaper, .edbzdtalk.

Benzodiazepine taper rates

Joint guideline, 2025:

- Reduce 5 to 10 percent of the current dose every 2 to 4 weeks.
- Do not exceed 25 percent every 2 weeks.
- Strong physiologic dependence: 5 to 10 percent every 6 to 8 weeks, or slower.
- Steps of 10 to 25 percent are reserved for lower doses and use under 3 months.
- If withdrawal is troublesome, pause or slow the taper first.
- Offer CBT for anxiety or CBT-I for insomnia during the taper.

Older deprescribing algorithm, 2018: about 25 percent every 2 weeks, then 12.5 percent near the end and planned drug-free days. This is faster than the 2025 guideline.

Switching a short-acting drug to a long-acting one such as diazepam before tapering is the Ashton Manual approach. It is optional. Equivalents: .edbzdequiv.

Withdrawal: anxiety, insomnia, tremor, sweating, and perceptual changes. Seizures are a risk with abrupt or rapid reduction.

title: Talking with inherited benzodiazepine patients
section: Physician education: opioids, benzodiazepines, and deprescribing
usage: Use as a physician reference for the first conversation with a patient inherited on long-term benzodiazepines. Not for the chart.

Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Talking with inherited benzodiazepine patients

Before the visit: send $bzdlet, check the PDMP, and calculate the diazepam equivalent.

At the visit:

- Start with reassurance: no one will stop the medicine suddenly.
- Ask what the medicine does for them now, and what they worry about if it changes.
- Name the patient's own risks: falls, memory, driving, opioid or alcohol co-use, sleep apnea.
- Explain dependence plainly: the body adapts, and the medicine often stops working as well over time.
- Offer choices rather than a deadline: taper now, taper later, or continue with risk reduction.
- If they agree to taper, start slowly and promise pauses. Give $pibzd and $pibzdtaper.
- Treat the underlying anxiety or insomnia with CBT, CBT-I, or an SSRI or SNRI.
- Document the shared decision, then reassess at least every 3 months.

Why patient education first: in EMPOWER, a mailed patient brochure alone led 27 percent of older adults to stop, vs 5 percent with usual care.

section: Physician education: opioids, benzodiazepines, and deprescribing
usage: Use as a physician reference on the 2023 Beers Criteria for older adults. Not for the chart.
cerner_text:

Beers Criteria 2023, key avoid items

- First-generation antihistamines: avoid
- Benzodiazepines: avoid, with exceptions such as seizures, REM sleep behavior disorder, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, severe generalized anxiety
- Z-drugs, eszopiclone, zaleplon, zolpidem: avoid
- Strongly anticholinergic antidepressants: amitriptyline, amoxapine, clomipramine, desipramine, doxepin over 6 mg/day, imipramine, nortriptyline, paroxetine: avoid
- Antimuscarinics for incontinence, such as oxybutynin and tolterodine: strongly anticholinergic, oxybutynin has the best evidence for cognitive harm
- Skeletal muscle relaxants: avoid, except baclofen or tizanidine for spasticity
- Chronic NSAIDs: avoid unless alternatives fail and a gastroprotective agent is used; indomethacin and ketorolac: avoid
- Sulfonylureas, all: avoid as first- or second-line or add-on unless substantial barriers; if used, choose short-acting such as glipizide
- Sliding-scale insulin without basal insulin: avoid
- Aspirin for primary prevention: avoid starting, consider deprescribing
- Warfarin as initial therapy for AF or VTE: avoid unless DOACs are contraindicated
- Rivaroxaban for long-term AF or VTE: avoid in favor of safer alternatives
- Dabigatran: use caution over other DOACs
- Digoxin: avoid as first line for AF or HF; if used, avoid over 0.125 mg/day
- Nifedipine immediate release: avoid
- Peripheral alpha-1 blockers as antihypertensives: avoid
- PPIs: avoid scheduled use over 8 weeks unless high risk
- Antipsychotics for dementia behaviors: avoid unless nonpharmacologic options fail or there is a threat of harm
- Systemic estrogen: do not start, consider deprescribing; low-dose vaginal estrogen is acceptable
- Megestrol: avoid
- Metoclopramide: avoid unless for gastroparesis, no more than 12 weeks
- Meperidine: avoid
- Oral mineral oil: avoid
- Desmopressin for nocturia: avoid
- Nitrofurantoin: avoid if CrCl under 30 or for long-term suppression
- Combinations to avoid: opioid plus gabapentinoid, opioid plus benzodiazepine

Alternatives: .edbeersswap. Kidney dosing: .edbeersrenal.

Source:

- AGS 2023 Beers Criteria Update Expert Panel. J Am Geriatr Soc 2023;71(7):2052-2081. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12478568/

title: Switch this to that
section: Physician education: opioids, benzodiazepines, and deprescribing
usage: Use as a physician reference for safer alternatives to Beers medications. Not for the chart.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Switch this to that, older adults

- Diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, chlorpheniramine for allergy: intranasal steroid, saline, loratadine, fexofenadine, or cetirizine
- Diphenhydramine or doxylamine for sleep: CBT-I; doxepin 6 mg/day or less if a drug is needed
- Benzodiazepine for anxiety: SSRI other than paroxetine, SNRI, buspirone, CBT; taper per .edbzdtaper
- Benzodiazepine or Z-drug for insomnia: CBT-I; taper, do not stop abruptly
- Amitriptyline or other tertiary TCA for depression: SSRI other than paroxetine, SNRI, or bupropion
- TCA for neuropathic pain: SNRI, gabapentin or pregabalin dosed for kidney function, topical lidocaine or capsaicin
- Paroxetine: sertraline or escitalopram
- Cyclobenzaprine, methocarbamol, carisoprodol: acetaminophen, topical NSAID, heat, PT
- Chronic oral NSAID: acetaminophen, topical diclofenac; if an NSAID is needed, shortest course with a PPI
- Glyburide or glimepiride: metformin, SGLT2i, GLP-1 RA, or DPP-4i; if a sulfonylurea is needed, glipizide
- Sliding-scale insulin alone: basal insulin with correction
- Aspirin for primary prevention: deprescribe
- Warfarin, new start: a DOAC such as apixaban, avoiding rivaroxaban
- Rivaroxaban for long-term AF or VTE: a safer DOAC such as apixaban
- Nifedipine immediate release: amlodipine or nifedipine extended release
- Doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin, or clonidine for hypertension: thiazide, ACEi, ARB, or long-acting dihydropyridine CCB
- Digoxin over 0.125 mg/day: lower dose, or a beta blocker for rate control
- Long-term PPI without a high-risk indication: step down to the lowest dose, on-demand use, or famotidine dosed for kidney function
- Oxybutynin or tolterodine for overactive bladder: bladder training, pelvic floor PT; mirabegron or vibegron are not on the Beers list
- Meperidine: another opioid at the lowest effective dose
- Oral mineral oil: polyethylene glycol
- Systemic estrogen for genitourinary symptoms: vaginal estrogen; for hot flashes, SSRI, SNRI, or gabapentin
- Desiccated thyroid: levothyroxine
- Megestrol for appetite: no drug alternative; address causes and nutrition
- Antipsychotic for dementia behaviors: nonpharmacologic approaches first
- Desmopressin for nocturia: evening fluid limits and treat the cause

Sources:

- Hanlon JT et al. J Am Geriatr Soc 2015;63(12):e8-e18. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26447889/
- AGS 2023 Beers Criteria: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12478568/

title: Talking about pediatric obesity
section: Physician education: pediatric obesity and Tulsa resources
usage: Use as a physician reference on how to discuss weight with children and families. Not for the chart.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Talking about pediatric obesity

Words:

- Ask permission first: "Is it OK if we talk about weight today?"
- Use neutral words: weight, healthy weight, BMI. Parents rate weight and unhealthy weight as most acceptable.
- Avoid obese, fat, extremely obese, and large. Families rate these most stigmatizing and least motivating.
- Ask which words the family prefers and use them; preferences vary by family.
- Use person-first language: a child with obesity, not an obese child.

Approach:

- Family-centered and non-stigmatizing; name the biologic, social, and structural drivers.
- Motivational interviewing: open questions, reflect, let the family choose 1 or 2 goals.
- Focus on health and habits, not weight loss or appearance.
- Ask about weight-based bullying and teasing at school and home.
- Screen for disordered eating before and during treatment.
- Weight stigma does not motivate change. It worsens binge eating, isolation, care avoidance, inactivity, and weight gain.

Treatment ladder:

- Intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment for age 6 and older, may offer age 2 to 5. Dose: 26 or more hours of family-based treatment over 3 to 12 months.
- Pharmacotherapy offered at age 12 and older.
- Metabolic and bariatric surgery evaluation at age 13 and older with severe obesity, BMI 120 percent of the 95th percentile or higher.
- Labs and BP: #wuobesk. Family handout: $piobesk. Tulsa programs: .edtulsaobes.

Sources:

- Hampl SE et al. AAP Clinical Practice Guideline on obesity. Pediatrics 2023;151(2):e2022060640. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36622115/
- Pont SJ et al. Stigma experienced by children and adolescents with obesity. Pediatrics 2017;140(6):e20173034. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29158228/
- Puhl RM et al. Parental perceptions of weight terminology. Pediatrics 2011;128(4):e786-793. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21949145/
- Puhl RM et al. Patient and family perspectives on terms for obesity. Pediatrics 2022;150(6). https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36404759/

title: Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir dosing
usage: Use as a reference when prescribing nirmatrelvir-ritonavir.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Start within 5 days of symptom onset in patients at high risk of progression. Run an interaction check first, ritonavir affects many drugs.

title: Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia reference
usage: Use as a refresher on current newborn bilirubin thresholds and phototherapy decisions.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Use the AAP 2022 hour-specific phototherapy and exchange thresholds by gestational age and neurotoxicity risk factors, for example in BiliTool.
Fixed thresholds such as 15 to 20 mg/dL in term infants, or exchange when TSB exceeds weight in kg times 10, are outdated.

Neurotoxicity risk factors:

- Gestational age under 38 weeks
- Albumin under 3 g/dL
- Isoimmune hemolytic disease, G6PD deficiency, or other hemolysis
- Sepsis
- Significant clinical instability in the past 24 hours

Escalation of care starts when TSB is within 2 mg/dL of the exchange threshold: TSB every 2 hours, intensive phototherapy, NICU involvement, and IVIG if isoimmune.
Stop phototherapy when TSB falls at least 2 mg/dL below the threshold at initiation.
Check rebound TSB 6 to 12 hours after stopping. Check again the next day if phototherapy started before 48 hours, DAT positive, or known or suspected hemolysis. Otherwise check bilirubin the day after stopping. If readmitted after discharge without birth-hospital phototherapy, or treated with home phototherapy, check bilirubin or follow up clinically 1 to 2 days after stopping.
