title: Failure to thrive and pediatric malnutrition reference
usage: Use as a refresher on catch-up calories, expected weight gain, and malnutrition severity.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Routine labs and imaging are low yield in failure to thrive. Let history and exam guide testing.
If testing is warranted, start with CBC, CMP, and UA, and consider TSH, celiac serology, and lead level.

Calories:

- Catch-up kcal/kg/day = RDA kcal/kg/day for weight-age x ideal weight for length in kg / actual weight in kg
- Catch-up growth often needs about 1.5 times usual calories until prior percentiles are regained
- Breast milk and standard term formula are about 20 kcal/oz
- Preterm transitional formula is 22 kcal/oz and preterm formula is 24 kcal/oz
- 1 oz is about 30 mL

Expected weight gain:

- 0 to 3 months: 25 to 35 g/day
- 3 to 6 months: 15 to 21 g/day
- 6 to 9 months: 12 to 13 g/day
- 9 to 12 months: about 9 g/day
- 1 to 3 years: 7 to 9 g/day

Malnutrition severity, single data point:

- Mild: weight for length or BMI z score -1 to -1.9
- Moderate: z score -2 to -2.9
- Severe: z score -3 or lower

Malnutrition severity, two or more data points:

- Mild: under 2 years, weight gain under 75 percent of expected; 2 to 20 years, weight loss of 5 percent of usual weight; decline of 1 z score; intake 51 to 75 percent of need
- Moderate: weight gain under 50 percent of expected; weight loss of 7.5 percent; decline of 2 z scores; intake 26 to 50 percent of need
- Severe: weight gain under 25 percent of expected; weight loss of 10 percent; decline of 3 z scores; intake under 26 percent of need

Weight checks: under 1 month old weekly, under 6 months every 2 to 4 weeks, under 12 months every 4 weeks. Check more often until gaining well.

title: Rupture of membranes testing reference
usage: Use as a refresher on the accuracy and pitfalls of ROM tests in triage.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

- Sterile speculum: look for pooling in the posterior fornix, with cough or Valsalva
- Nitrazine: blue means pH over 6.5. Sensitive, but false positives are common with blood, semen, bacterial vaginosis, trichomonas, urine, and soap. False negatives occur with intermittent leak or dilute fluid
- Ferning: swab the posterior fornix, not the cervix, and air-dry on a slide for 10 minutes. A fine fern pattern suggests amniotic fluid; cervical mucus gives thick, wide arborization
- PAMG-1 or IGFBP-1 immunoassay, such as AmniSure: high sensitivity and little effect from trace blood or semen. False positives can occur with intact membranes, especially in labor. Use when standard tests are equivocal
- Ultrasound: low amniotic fluid supports but does not confirm ROM
- Avoid digital cervical exams in suspected PPROM unless in active labor or delivery is imminent

title: Joint injection mixtures reference
usage: Use as a refresher on typical steroid and lidocaine volumes by injection site.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

K40 is triamcinolone acetonide 40 mg/mL, M40 is methylprednisolone acetate 40 mg/mL, and L is 1 or 2 percent lidocaine without epinephrine.

- Subacromial bursa: 1 mL K40 plus 4 mL L
- AC joint: 0.25 to 0.5 mL K40 plus 0.5 to 1 mL L
- Olecranon bursa: 0.5 mL K40 plus 1 to 2 mL L
- Lateral epicondyle: 1 mL M40 plus 2 mL L
- Greater trochanteric bursa: 1 mL K40 plus 4 mL L
- Knee: 1 mL K40 plus 2 to 5 mL L
- Ankle: 1 mL M40 plus 1 mL L
- Plantar fascia: 1 mL K40 plus 2 mL L
- Trigger point: lidocaine alone preferred, 1 to 3 mL L

Lateral epicondyle steroid injections give short-term relief but worse outcomes at 6 to 12 months than physical therapy or waiting.
Plantar fascia steroid injections carry a risk of fascia rupture and fat pad atrophy.
Space steroid injections into the same joint at least 3 months apart.
Steroid injections raise blood glucose for several days in patients with diabetes.

K40 is triamcinolone acetonide 40 mg/mL, M40 is methylprednisolone acetate 40 mg/mL, and L is 1 or 2 percent lidocaine without epinephrine.

- Subacromial bursa: 1 mL K40 plus 4 mL L
- AC joint: 0.25 to 0.5 mL K40 plus 0.5 to 1 mL L
- Olecranon bursa: 0.5 mL K40 plus 1 to 2 mL L
- Lateral epicondyle: 1 mL M40 plus 2 mL L
- Greater trochanteric bursa: 1 mL K40 plus 4 mL L
- Knee: 1 mL K40 plus 2 to 5 mL L
- Ankle: 1 mL M40 plus 1 mL L
- Plantar fascia: 1 mL K40 plus 2 mL L
- Trigger point: lidocaine alone preferred, 1 to 3 mL L

Lateral epicondyle steroid injections give short-term relief but worse outcomes at 6 to 12 months than physical therapy or waiting.
Plantar fascia steroid injections carry a risk of fascia rupture and fat pad atrophy.
Space steroid injections into the same joint at least 3 months apart.
Steroid injections raise blood glucose for several days in patients with diabetes.

title: Acute kidney injury reference
usage: Use as a refresher on AKI staging, workup, and causes.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

KDIGO definition, any one of:

- Creatinine rise of 0.3 mg/dL or more within 48 hours
- Creatinine 1.5 times baseline within 7 days
- Urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours

KDIGO stages:

- Stage 1: creatinine 1.5 to 1.9 times baseline or a rise of 0.3 or more. Or urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 to 12 hours
- Stage 2: creatinine 2.0 to 2.9 times baseline, or urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/h for 12 hours or more
- Stage 3: creatinine 3 times baseline or 4.0 or more, or dialysis. Or urine output under 0.3 mL/kg/h for 24 hours, or anuria for 12 hours

Approach:

- Look first for an obvious cause: hypotension, volume loss, nephrotoxins, contrast, obstruction
- Send UA with microscopy and urine sodium, creatinine, and urea before fluids or diuretics when possible
- Bladder scan, then renal ultrasound if obstruction is possible or the cause is unclear
- Volume depleted: isotonic crystalloid, reassess in 12 to 24 hours
- Volume overloaded: loop diuretic trial, reassess
- Stop NSAIDs and nephrotoxins, hold ACE inhibitor, ARB, and diuretics if hypovolemic, renally dose all drugs
- Nephrology for unclear intrinsic cause, active sediment, stage 3, or dialysis indications; urology for obstruction
- Dialysis indications: refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, or volume overload, uremic pericarditis or encephalopathy, dialyzable toxins

Urine indices:

- FENa under 1 percent suggests prerenal, over 2 percent suggests ATN
- FEUrea under 35 percent suggests prerenal and stays reliable after diuretics
- Muddy brown granular casts suggest ATN, red cell casts suggest glomerulonephritis, white cell casts suggest interstitial nephritis or pyelonephritis
- Urine eosinophils are inaccurate for interstitial nephritis and are not recommended

Creatinine lags the fall in GFR by 24 to 48 hours.
NSAIDs block prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation and worsen prerenal AKI, especially with an ACE inhibitor or ARB plus a diuretic.

Causes:

- Prerenal: GI, renal, or skin losses, hemorrhage, heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypotension or sepsis, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitor or ARB, hypercalcemia, hepatorenal syndrome
- Intrinsic: ATN from ischemia, contrast, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, amphotericin, cisplatin, rhabdomyolysis, or hemolysis; interstitial nephritis from beta-lactams, sulfonamides, PPIs, NSAIDs, or rifampin; glomerulonephritis from infection, lupus, or vasculitis; thrombotic microangiopathy
- Postrenal: stones, clots, papillary necrosis, tumor, retroperitoneal fibrosis, neurogenic bladder, BPH, prostate cancer, urethral stricture, phimosis

Contrast prophylaxis is for AKI or eGFR under 30, not on dialysis. Give normal saline 1 to 3 mL/kg/h from 1 hour before to 3 to 12 hours after the study.

title: Anticoagulant reversal reference
usage: Use as a refresher on reversal agents and doses for bleeding or procedures on anticoagulants.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Use the local order set _ local and confirm doses with pharmacy.

- Unfractionated heparin: protamine 1 mg IV per 100 units of heparin given in the last 2 to 3 hours, max 50 mg, given slowly
- Enoxaparin within 8 hours: protamine 1 mg IV per 1 mg of enoxaparin, max 50 mg; 0.5 mg per 1 mg if 8 to 12 hours; reversal is partial
- Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g IV, given as two 2.5 g doses no more than 15 minutes apart
- Apixaban or rivaroxaban: 4-factor PCC 25 to 50 units/kg IV once; andexanet alfa is no longer sold in the US
- Edoxaban: 4-factor PCC 25 to 50 units/kg IV once
- Argatroban or bivalirudin: stop the infusion, short half-life, no specific reversal agent
- Warfarin with major bleeding: vitamin K 10 mg IV once plus 4-factor PCC IV once. Plasma only if PCC is unavailable
- PCC dose: INR 2 to under 4, 25 units/kg, max 2500 units. INR 4 to 6, 35 units/kg, max 3500 units. INR over 6, 50 units/kg, max 5000 units
- Warfarin, INR 4.5 to 10 without bleeding: hold warfarin, vitamin K not routinely needed
- Warfarin, INR over 10 without bleeding: hold warfarin and give vitamin K 2.5 to 5 mg PO once
- Warfarin before a procedure in 24 to 48 hours: vitamin K 1 to 2.5 mg PO once, recheck INR

title: CAP admission reference
usage: Use as a reference while admitting community-acquired pneumonia; the chart block is separate.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

CAP admission checklist

Severe CAP is 1 major criterion, septic shock needing pressors or mechanical ventilation, or 3 or more minor criteria:

- RR 30 or higher
- PaO2/FiO2 250 or lower
- Multilobar infiltrates
- Confusion
- BUN 20 or higher
- WBC under 4,000
- Platelets under 100,000
- Temperature under 36 C
- Hypotension needing aggressive fluids

Triage: CURB-65 and PSI for site of care.

Chart check: lung disease, baseline O2, prior cultures, antibiotics in the last 90 days, allergies, influenza and pneumococcal vaccines.

Cannot miss: hypoxemic respiratory failure, sepsis, PE, ACS, empyema.

History:

- Symptoms: onset and course, dyspnea, cough, sputum, fever, rigors, pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss, diarrhea
- Exposures: sick contacts, travel, animals, occupation, TB, recent healthcare or antibiotics, smoking
- MRSA risk: prior MRSA, post-influenza, IV drug use, cavitary disease, positive nasal swab
- Pseudomonas risk: prior isolation, bronchiectasis, severe COPD, immunosuppression, recent hospitalization with IV antibiotics
- Aspiration risk: dementia, altered mental status, alcohol or drug use, dysphagia, poor dentition, bedbound

Exam: work of breathing, O2 need, crackles, decreased breath sounds, egophony, dullness to percussion, rash, edema.

DDx:

- Infectious: viral such as COVID, influenza, RSV; bacterial such as pneumococcus, H influenzae, Moraxella, Legionella, Mycoplasma, MRSA, Pseudomonas; fungal such as PJP, histoplasmosis, aspergillus
- Noninfectious pulmonary: aspiration pneumonitis, atelectasis, PE, organizing pneumonia, ILD, malignancy, drug pneumonitis, alveolar hemorrhage
- Cardiac: heart failure, ACS
- Other: vasculitis, lupus, sarcoidosis, acute chest syndrome

Workup: CXR for all. CT if PE concern, unclear diagnosis, or complications. MRSA nares PCR. Blood and sputum cultures if severe or MRSA or Pseudomonas risk. Urine Legionella and pneumococcal antigens if severe. Procalcitonin and viral panel as adjuncts.

Treatment:

- Ward, no resistant-organism risk: beta-lactam plus macrolide. Ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g IV daily or ampicillin-sulbactam 1.5 to 3 g IV every 6 hours, plus azithromycin 500 mg IV or PO daily
- Or levofloxacin 750 mg IV or PO daily alone
- Doxycycline 100 mg IV or PO BID in place of azithromycin only if macrolides and fluoroquinolones are both contraindicated
- Pseudomonas: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours, cefepime 2 g IV every 8 hours, or meropenem 1 g IV every 8 hours
- MRSA: vancomycin dosed by pharmacy, or linezolid 600 mg IV or PO every 12 hours
- Severe CAP without influenza: hydrocortisone 50 mg IV every 6 hours
- Duration: nonsevere CAP, 3 to 5 days once clinically stable; severe CAP, at least 5 days; 7 days for MRSA or Pseudomonas
- Drain large or loculated parapneumonic effusions and all empyemas
- Supportive: acetaminophen, incentive spirometry, benzonatate 100 mg PO TID as needed
- Discharge when afebrile 48 hours, at baseline O2, and vitals stable

title: Dizziness differential
usage: Use as a reference when sorting out a dizziness complaint.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Dizziness differential by type

Vertigo, a false sense of motion:

- BPPV: brief and positional, Dix-Hallpike or supine roll test
- Vestibular neuritis or labyrinthitis: continuous for days, hearing loss in labyrinthitis
- Meniere disease: episodes lasting hours with hearing loss, tinnitus, aural fullness
- Vestibular migraine
- Head trauma
- Posterior circulation stroke: acute continuous vertigo with any central sign, HINTS only if trained, otherwise image

Disequilibrium, feeling off balance:

- Peripheral neuropathy, Parkinson disease, cerebellar disease, medications, stroke, vision loss

Presyncope, near fainting:

- Orthostatic hypotension, including from medications
- Arrhythmia, structural heart disease, ACS
- Volume loss, anemia

Lightheadedness, vague:

- Anxiety, depression, hyperventilation, medication effect, hypoglycemia

Central red flags: new headache, neck pain, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia, limb weakness or numbness, inability to walk, vascular risk factors.

Routine labs and imaging are low yield without neurologic findings. Target testing to the suspected cause.

ECG, ambulatory monitoring, and carotid imaging only if a cardiac or vascular cause is suspected.

title: Newborn hyperbilirubinemia risk factors
usage: Use as a reference when deciding newborn bilirubin follow-up and treatment thresholds.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Newborn hyperbilirubinemia, AAP 2022 approach

Use hour-specific phototherapy and exchange thresholds by gestational age and neurotoxicity risk factors, such as BiliTool. The old risk-zone nomogram and race-based risk are no longer used.

Risk factors for significant hyperbilirubinemia:

- Lower gestational age, risk rises below 40 weeks
- Jaundice in the first 24 hours
- Predischarge TcB or TSB close to the phototherapy threshold
- Hemolysis, known or suspected from a rise of 0.3 mg/dL/hour or more in the first 24 hours or 0.2 mg/dL/hour or more after
- Phototherapy before discharge
- Parent or sibling who needed phototherapy or exchange transfusion
- Family history or ancestry suggesting an inherited red cell disorder, including G6PD deficiency
- Exclusive breastfeeding with suboptimal intake
- Scalp hematoma or significant bruising
- Down syndrome
- Macrosomic infant of a diabetic mother

Neurotoxicity risk factors, which lower the treatment threshold:

- Gestational age under 38 weeks, risk rises as age falls
- Albumin under 3.0 g/dL
- Isoimmune hemolytic disease, G6PD deficiency, or other hemolytic condition
- Sepsis
- Significant clinical instability in the previous 24 hours

title: OB triage by complaint
usage: Use as a reference when working up common OB triage complaints.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

OB triage by complaint

Term labor rule-out:

- Ask about contraction onset, frequency and intensity, and prior cesarean
- Bedside US for presentation
- Active labor begins at 6 cm; admit for active labor, cervical change with regular painful contractions, or ROM
- No cervical change on repeat SVE in 1 to 2 hours: discharge with labor precautions

Leakage of fluid, term or preterm:

- Ask about timing, intercourse in the past 24 hours, bleeding, discharge odor, and contractions
- Differential: ROM, cervical mucus, vaginitis or cervicitis, urinary incontinence, sweat
- Sterile speculum: look for pooling, have the patient cough or Valsalva
- Nitrazine: blue is positive, sensitivity about 90 percent, false positives with blood, semen, soap, or vaginitis
- Fern: swab posterior fornix, dry 10 minutes, a delicate fern pattern is positive
- PAMG-1 test such as AmniSure if equivocal, sensitivity and specificity about 98 percent
- Ultrasound AFI or MVP if still unclear
- GBS culture if 36 weeks or later and status unknown, GC and chlamydia, vaginal panel as indicated

Preterm labor rule-out:

- Ask about prior preterm birth, prior cesarean, and steroids this pregnancy
- Sterile speculum first, UA with culture, GC and chlamydia, vaginal panel, GBS culture
- Under 34 weeks with cervix under 3 cm and intact membranes: transvaginal cervical length
- Cervical length under 20 mm: admit for observation, steroids, and plan with OB hospitalist; over 30 mm: preterm labor unlikely; 20 to 30 mm: send fFN if no bleeding, ROM, exam, or intercourse in 24 hours
- Cervix over 3 cm, effacement over 80 percent, ROM, bleeding, or persistent painful contractions: admit
- Preterm labor at 24w0d to 33w6d: betamethasone 12 mg IM q24h for 2 doses, GBS prophylaxis, short tocolysis to complete steroids
- Under 32 weeks: magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 20 minutes, then 1 g/hour IV for neuroprotection
- 34w0d to 36w6d: consider betamethasone if delivery likely within 7 days, no prior course, and no pregestational diabetes
- 34 weeks or later: SVE after discussion with senior or attending, discuss findings with the OB hospitalist
- 17-hydroxyprogesterone caproate was withdrawn in 2023, do not offer it

Elevated BP, rule out preeclampsia:

- Ask about headache, vision changes, RUQ pain, dyspnea, prior HTN or preeclampsia, aspirin use, and MFM care
- Measure BP seated or semi-reclined, arm at heart level, after 10 minutes of rest
- Labs: CBC, CMP, urine protein to creatinine ratio, LDH if HELLP suspected
- Preeclampsia at 37 weeks or later: delivery; earlier, admit and plan with OB hospitalist
- BP q15min; severe range 160/110 or higher lasting 15 minutes needs treatment within 30 to 60 minutes

Decreased fetal movement:

- Differential: fetal sleep, maternal medications or tobacco, oligohydramnios, fetal compromise
- NST, then AFI or BPP if NST nonreactive or risk factors present
- Admit for oligohydramnios or persistently nonreactive or nonreassuring testing
- If reassuring, discharge with kick count teaching: 10 movements within 2 hours at rest

Antepartum bleeding:

- Differential: abruption, previa, vasa previa, cervicitis, trauma, labor
- Ultrasound for placental location before any digital exam, then speculum exam
- CBC, type and screen, coags, fibrinogen; Kleihauer-Betke and RhIG if Rh negative
- Nonreassuring FHT suggests abruption; admit for previa, abruption, or labor

title: Perioperative anticoagulation
usage: Use as a reference when planning anticoagulant holds and restarts around procedures.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Perioperative anticoagulation

Procedure bleeding risk:

- Minimal: dental, cataract, minor skin; continue anticoagulant or skip one DOAC dose
- Low to moderate: most procedures under 45 minutes
- High: major surgery, neuraxial anesthesia, kidney or liver biopsy, procedures over 45 minutes

DOAC hold, no bridging:

- Apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban: hold 1 day before low bleed risk and 2 days before high bleed risk procedures
- Dabigatran, CrCl 50 or more: hold 1 day before low and 2 days before high bleed risk; CrCl under 50: hold 2 days before low and 4 days before high bleed risk
- Restart 24 hours after low bleed risk and 48 to 72 hours after high bleed risk procedures once hemostasis is secure

Warfarin:

- Hold 5 days before, check INR the day before, vitamin K 1 to 2 mg PO once if INR 1.5 or higher
- Restart 12 to 24 hours after surgery at usual dose if hemostasis secure
- Bridge only if very high thrombotic risk: mechanical mitral valve, older mechanical aortic valve, stroke or TIA within 3 months, VTE within 3 months, or severe thrombophilia
- Most atrial fibrillation patients should not be bridged, even with high CHA2DS2-VASc
- Bridging: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcut q12h, last dose 24 hours before surgery, resume 48 to 72 hours after high bleed risk procedures

Emergencies:

- Hold anticoagulant, check timing of last dose and renal function
- Dabigatran reversal: idarucizumab 5 g IV once
- Factor Xa inhibitor reversal: 4-factor PCC per _ local protocol; andexanet alfa is no longer sold in the US
- Warfarin reversal: 4-factor PCC per INR and weight plus vitamin K 10 mg IV once

title: Seizure and status epilepticus
usage: Use as a reference when evaluating a seizure or managing status epilepticus.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Seizure and status epilepticus

Provoked seizure causes:

- Alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, drug intoxication or withdrawal
- Antiseizure medication nonadherence
- Hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia, hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, uremia
- CNS infection, stroke, hemorrhage, mass

Epilepsy risk factors:

- Febrile seizures in infancy, family history of epilepsy
- Prior TBI, stroke, subdural hematoma, anoxic injury, CNS infection, neurodegenerative disease, tumor

Status epilepticus is a seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer, or recurrent seizures without return to baseline.

- ABCs, monitors, fingerstick glucose, IV access
- Thiamine 100 mg IV before glucose if alcohol use or malnutrition, dextrose 50% 50 mL IV if glucose under 60
- Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV, max 4 mg per dose, may repeat once in 5 minutes
- No IV: midazolam 10 mg IM once if over 40 kg, 5 mg IM if 13 to 40 kg
- Second line, choose one:
- Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV, max 4500 mg
- Valproate 40 mg/kg IV, max 3000 mg
- Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV, max 1500 mg PE
- Refractory: intubate, continuous midazolam or propofol infusion, continuous EEG, neurology and ICU
- Not back to baseline after the expected postictal period: consider nonconvulsive status, get EEG

Seizure mimics:

- Convulsive syncope, rigors, myoclonus, migraine, posturing
- Functional or psychogenic nonepileptic spells: involve neurology, supportive approach, avoid overtesting; can coexist with epilepsy

Medications that lower seizure threshold:

- Tramadol, bupropion, antipsychotics, some SSRIs
- Fluoroquinolones, high-dose penicillins, cefepime, carbapenems
- Abrupt benzodiazepine or barbiturate withdrawal

Workup:

- CMP, magnesium, phosphorus, glucose, CBC, tox screen, antiseizure drug levels, pregnancy test
- LP if infection suspected
- CT head without contrast for acute hemorrhage, then MRI brain with and without contrast, seizure protocol
- EEG, continuous for status or to characterize spells

title: Rome IV IBS criteria
usage: Use when deciding whether chronic abdominal pain with bowel change meets IBS criteria and which subtype.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Recurrent abdominal pain on average at least 1 day/week in the last 3 months. Onset at least 6 months before diagnosis. Plus 2 or more of:

- Related to defecation
- Associated with a change in stool frequency
- Associated with a change in stool form

Subtype by stool form on days with abnormal stools:

- IBS-C: over 25% Bristol 1-2 and under 25% Bristol 6-7
- IBS-D: over 25% Bristol 6-7 and under 25% Bristol 1-2
- IBS-M: over 25% Bristol 1-2 and over 25% Bristol 6-7
- IBS-U: meets criteria but does not fit a subtype

Alarm features that need further workup: age 45 or older at onset, weight loss, GI bleeding, iron deficiency anemia, nocturnal symptoms, family history of colon cancer, celiac disease or IBD.

title: Abdominal pain approach
usage: Use when building a differential for abdominal pain.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Pain types:

- Somatic: sharp, well localized, reproducible, from skin, muscle or parietal peritoneum
- Neuropathic: burning or pins and needles from nerve injury, for example zoster or radiculopathy
- Visceral: vague, diffuse, from capsular stretch or hollow viscus obstruction

Visceral patterns:

- Obstruction of bowel, ureter or biliary tree: colicky, patient writhes to find comfort, little fever or leukocytosis
- Inflammation such as pancreatitis, cholecystitis, pyelonephritis, diverticulitis: constant pain, mild fever and leukocytosis
- Perforation: patient lies still, peritoneal signs, marked fever and leukocytosis
- Ischemia: pain out of proportion to exam, surgical emergency
- Referred pain from chest, pelvis or spine

By quadrant and first imaging:

- RUQ, ultrasound first: liver, gallbladder, duodenum, lung base, diaphragm
- RLQ, CT first, ultrasound first in children and pregnancy: appendix, colon, kidney and ureter, ovary or testis
- LUQ, CT: spleen, stomach, pancreas tail, lung base, diaphragm
- LLQ, CT: diverticulitis, colon, kidney and ureter, ovary or testis
- Pelvic ultrasound for suspected ovarian torsion, ectopic pregnancy or adnexal mass

Medical causes: DKA, uremia, hypercalcemia, adrenal insufficiency, porphyria, lead poisoning, hereditary angioedema, acute angle-closure glaucoma.

Consider ACS in upper abdominal pain, and pregnancy testing in anyone who could be pregnant.

title: Dyspnea differential
usage: Use when evaluating acute dyspnea, including on night call.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Differential by system:

- Acid-base: metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
- Blood: anemia, carbon monoxide or methemoglobinemia
- Cardiac: heart failure, arrhythmia, ACS, tamponade, valve disease
- Airway and lung: asthma, COPD, pneumonia, pneumothorax, pleural effusion, ILD, alveolar hemorrhage, ARDS, tumor, aspiration, anaphylaxis
- Vascular: pulmonary embolism
- Other: neuromuscular weakness, anxiety

First tests on night call:

- ABG or VBG with co-oximetry for acid-base, CO and methemoglobin
- ECG for ischemia, arrhythmia and pericardial disease
- CXR for parenchymal, pleural and cardiac causes
- Add CBC, BNP, troponin and bedside ultrasound as indicated

These do not exclude PE; risk-stratify separately with Wells and D-dimer or CTPA.

title: Skin lesion terms
usage: Use when describing primary and secondary skin lesions.
cerner_text:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Primary lesions:

- Macule: flat color change up to 1 cm, not palpable, for example cafe au lait or ash leaf macule
- Patch: flat color change over 1 cm
- Papule: elevated solid lesion up to 1 cm, for example acne, warts, milia
- Plaque: elevated plateau-like solid lesion over 1 cm, for example psoriasis
- Nodule: elevated solid lesion over 1 cm with depth, for example cyst
- Vesicle: elevated fluid-filled lesion up to 1 cm, for example herpes simplex
- Bulla: elevated fluid-filled lesion over 1 cm, for example bullous impetigo
- Pustule: elevated pus-filled lesion, for example acne or erythema toxicum

Secondary lesions:

- Scale: excess stratum corneum, fine and branny, thick white and adherent as in psoriasis, or fish-scale-like
- Crust: dried serum, blood or pus over damaged epidermis, for example impetigo
- Erosion: partial loss of epidermis, heals without scarring
- Ulcer: full-thickness loss of epidermis into dermis, heals with scarring
- Fissure: linear painful break, often from dry skin
- Atrophy: thin, wrinkled skin with visible vessels, epidermal from topical steroids or dermal depression from injected steroids
- Scar: fibrous replacement after dermal injury, may be hypertrophic or atrophic
